messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

# Chinedu's Story

Chinedu was nine years old when his uncle came to stay with them in Lagos. The man had rough hands—palms calloused and scarred from years working construction—and a temper that ignited without warning. One afternoon, after Chinedu spilled water on the kitchen floor, his uncle grabbed him by the wrist, his grip a vise of heat and pressure. The skin of his uncle's palm was coarse, almost like sandpaper, and it burned against Chinedu's forearm as he was dragged into the back room. The beating that followed lasted only minutes, but the sensations lingered: the texture of that rough palm, the suffocating warmth of the room, the sound of footsteps approaching from behind whenever his uncle moved through the house. By the time his mother sent his uncle away three months later, Chinedu had learned to flinch at the sound of approaching footsteps, to feel his heart race when someone's skin—rough or warm—made contact with his own.

Now, at twenty-seven, Chinedu had built a life in Atlanta that kept him moving. He drove for Uber five nights a week, a job that suited him because it meant solitude, control, and constant motion. But the city itself had become a minefield of invisible triggers. The texture of a passenger's wool coat brushing his arm in the backseat could send him spiraling; the warmth of another body in close quarters made his skin crawl. Footsteps on the pavement behind him—a pedestrian approaching his car, a neighbor walking down the hallway of his apartment building—would snap his attention backward, his shoulders tensing, his breath shallow. These moments came without warning, and they came often. When a trigger hit, Chinedu's first instinct was to reach for his phone and scroll mindlessly through videos, anything to pull his attention away from the sensation still prickling on his skin. More frequently now, he was using cocaine—a habit that had started as occasional relief and had quietly become something he needed before difficult shifts. The drugs dulled the edge, made the world feel less sharp, less threatening. They also gave him something to focus on besides the fact that his body seemed determined to betray him, reacting as if danger were still present even when he knew, rationally, that he was safe in his apartment or alone in his car.

What frightened Chinedu most was the certainty that he had become irreparably broken. He had come to believe that something fundamental in him had shattered that day in Lagos, that no amount of time or distance would mend it. His body had turned against him—it kept reacting as if his uncle were still there, still reaching for him, still threatening. Even when passengers were kind, even when his sister called to check on him, even when he sat alone in his apartment with the doors locked, he could not silence the alarm bells ringing in his nervous system. This conviction fed everything else. Because he believed he was damaged beyond repair, because he felt unsafe even in objectively safe situations, he stopped trying to let people close. His sister had invited him to family gatherings, and he had declined every invitation for the past two years. The few women who had shown interest in him were met with coldness and withdrawal; he could not bear the thought of being touched, of being vulnerable, of someone discovering just how broken he really was. His hypervigilance—the constant scanning for threat, the way his eyes tracked movement in his rearview mirror, the way he sat with his back to the wall—had become exhausting and inescapable. Even when he was objectively safe, his mind and body insisted otherwise, and that impossibility of trusting safety, of ever truly relaxing, only deepened his conviction that he was permanently changed.

The hypervigilance and the inability to trust safety fed a reckless streak that had begun to alarm him. He was driving too fast on empty highways at night, taking passengers in neighborhoods he knew were dangerous, staying out until dawn without sleep. Part of him felt invincible, as if he had already been damaged so thoroughly that nothing worse could happen. Another part of him, quieter and more terrifying, wondered if he was unconsciously courting harm. The cocaine use had accelerated in recent weeks, and with it came a growing sense of isolation. He had lost touch with the Nigerian community he had once felt tethered to—the church his mother attended, the friends from university who still gathered on weekends. He could not explain to them why he could not be around people, why a casual touch made him recoil, why he was not the person they remembered. The drugs and the distraction, the avoidance of intimacy and the constant movement, had become a wall between him and everything that had once felt like home.

It was his sister who finally pushed him to seek help. She had noticed the weight loss, the tremor in his hands, the way he flinched when she tried to hug him. She had also learned, through a mutual friend, about the cocaine. When she confronted him three weeks ago, Chinedu had no defense—only the exhausted admission that he could not keep living this way, that something had to change. What he feared most was that therapy would confirm what he already believed: that he was beyond repair. What he hoped for, though he barely dared speak it aloud, was that someone might help him understand why his body would not believe he was safe, and whether there was any way to reclaim even a fraction of the person he had been before his uncle arrived.

violation_explanations: Triggers (texture, warmth, footsteps) are described as occurring, and maladaptive strategies (phone scrolling, cocaine use, avoidance) are described as occurring, but no paragraph explicitly conveys that the triggers directly drive or lead to the maladaptive strategies; the causal relationship is implied but not clearly stated within the same paragraph.

Negative appraisals ('irreparably broken', 'damaged beyond repair', 'permanently changed') and maladaptive strategies (avoidance of people, isolation, drug use) both appear, but no paragraph clearly conveys that the appraisals drive the strategies; the connection is thematic rather than causally explicit.

Threat (feeling unsafe, alarm bells in nervous system, hypervigilance) and maladaptive strategies (reckless driving, cocaine use, isolation) both appear, but no single paragraph clearly states that the sense of threat leads to or drives the maladaptive coping; the relationship is implicit rather than causally articulated.
